items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gross domestic product (GDP)"?
options: The average rate of growth of real GDP over a long period, reflecting the growth of potential output
An exchange rate that equalises the purchasing power of currencies so that the same basket of goods costs the same in each country
The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given time period, usually a year

The World Happiness Report ranking of countries by average life evaluations (the Cantril ladder), explained by GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceived corruption
items.answer: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given time period, usually a year
items.markingKey: C. "gross domestic product (GDP)" is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given time period, usually a year.

items.stem: Briefly explain why national income can be measured by the output, income and expenditure methods.
items.answer: Every unit of spending on final output becomes income for the factors that produced it, so in the circular flow total output = total income = total expenditure (allowing for statistical discrepancy).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every unit of spending on final output becomes income for the factors that produced it, so in the circular flow total output = total income = total expenditure (allowing for statistical discrepancy). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between GDP per capita and total GDP.
items.answer: Total GDP is the size of the whole economy; GDP per capita divides by population, so it shows average output per person and allows living-standard comparisons.
items.markingKey: Total GDP is the size of the whole economy; GDP per capita divides by population, so it shows average output per person and allows living-standard comparisons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the comparison of China and the USA using PPP as an example, explain purchasing power parity.
items.answer: At market exchange rates US GDP is larger than China's, but the IMF estimates China's GDP at PPP has exceeded the USA's since about 2016. Lower prices of non-traded goods in China mean each yuan buys more, so PPP raises China's measured output relative to market-rate figures
items.markingKey: Context (At market exchange rates US GDP is larger than China's, but the IMF estimates China's GDP at PPP has exceeded the USA's since about 2016.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower prices of non-traded goods in China mean each yuan buys more, so PPP raises China's measured output relative to market-rate figures – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to purchasing power parity.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2023 Luxembourg had one of the highest GDP per capita figures in the world, above $120,000. However, almost half of its workforce are cross-border commuters from France, Belgium and Germany, whose output is counted in Luxembourg's GDP although they live and spend much of their income elsewhere.
— Adapted from Eurostat and World Bank commentary

Using the extract, explain why GDP per capita may overstate the living standards of Luxembourg's residents.
items.answer: Output of cross-border commuters is in the numerator (GDP) but they are not in the population denominator, so GDP per capita is inflated; GNI per capita (which subtracts income paid to non-residents) is lower and better reflects residents' income.
items.markingKey: Output of cross-border commuters is in the numerator (GDP) but they are not in the population denominator, so GDP per capita is inflated; GNI per capita (which subtracts income paid to non-residents) is lower and better reflects residents' income. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
The national statistics office of Country X publishes the following expenditure data for last year (in $ billion): consumption 885, investment 150, government spending 299, exports 177, imports 342.
Net income from abroad is −$8 bn and the population is 8 million. Calculate GNI per capita, and explain why GNI per capita may be a better indicator of living standards than total GDP.
items.answer: GNI = $1161 bn; GNI per capita ≈ $145,125. Per capita measures adjust for population size, and GNI counts income that residents actually receive (it excludes profits repatriated by foreign firms).
items.markingKey: GDP = 1169; GNI = 1169 + (-8) = 1161 bn; per capita = 1161 × 10⁹ / (8 × 10⁶) = $145,125. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for ≈ $145,125. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [R1][R1] for the two explanation points (population; income received by residents).

items.stem: Country X has GDP of $50 bn, net income from abroad of −$4 bn and a population of 20 million. Country Y has GDP of $46 bn, net income from abroad of +$3 bn and a population of 14 million. Calculate GNI per capita for each country and explain which data you would use to judge which has the higher living standards.
items.answer: GNI X = $46 bn → $2,300 per person; GNI Y = $49 bn → $3,500 per person. Y appears better off; but use PPP-adjusted figures, distribution (Gini) and non-income indicators (HDI) before concluding.
items.markingKey: GNI X = $46 bn → $2,300 per person; GNI Y = $49 bn → $3,500 per person. Y appears better off; but use PPP-adjusted figures, distribution (Gini) and non-income indicators (HDI) before concluding.

items.stem: You are an adviser to the central bank. A minister argues that gNI per capita at PPP is the most useful single measure for comparing living standards between countries. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: It is the best single monetary measure, but comparisons should be supplemented by composite indicators such as the HDI and by inequality data.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: adjusts for population size; adjusts for price-level differences; includes net income from abroad, reflecting residents' incomes. Counter-points: ignores distribution of income; excludes non-market and informal output; ignores environmental costs, leisure and quality of life; PPP estimates rely on price surveys that may be inaccurate. Recommendation: It is the best single monetary measure, but comparisons should be supplemented by composite indicators such as the HDI and by inequality data. Policy recommendation markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) a clear recommendation that is justified with economic theory, the information provided and its likely consequences for stakeholders; trade-offs and risks weighed. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem: Which of the following is counted in GDP?
options: The sale of a second-hand house
A new car produced in the country and sold to a household
Shares bought on the stock exchange
items.answer: A new car produced in the country and sold to a household
items.markingKey: C. Only final goods and services produced in the period count; transfers and second-hand or financial transactions are excluded.

items.stem: Briefly explain why intermediate goods are excluded from GDP.
items.answer: Their value is already included in the price of the final good; counting them again would be double counting and overstate output. The value-added approach avoids this.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their value is already included in the price of the final good; counting them again would be double counting and overstate output. The value-added approach avoids this. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between real GDP and nominal GDP.
items.answer: Nominal GDP is valued at current prices and rises with inflation; real GDP is valued at constant prices, so it changes only when the volume of output changes.
items.markingKey: Nominal GDP is valued at current prices and rises with inflation; real GDP is valued at constant prices, so it changes only when the volume of output changes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: World Bank data for Halvania: GDP per capita 600,000 ZD; official exchange rate 40 ZD/$; PPP conversion factor 10 ZD/int$. Calculate GDP per capita at (i) the market exchange rate and (ii) purchasing power parity, and explain the difference.
items.answer: (i) $15,000; (ii) int$60,000. PPP is higher because prices of non-traded goods and services are lower in Halvania, so each unit of currency buys more domestically.
items.markingKey: (i) 600,000/40 = $15,000; (ii) 600,000/10 = int$60,000. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for $15,000 and int$60,000. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [R1] PPP adjusts for differences in the cost of living, which are typically lower in lower-income economies.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the output, income and expenditure methods of measuring national income must give the same value.
items.answer: Circular flow: the value of output equals the incomes paid to factors and the spending on that output; diagram with households, firms, government, financial sector and foreign sector.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Circular flow: the value of output equals the incomes paid to factors and the spending on that output; diagram with households, firms, government, financial sector and foreign sector. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

Irish GDP was revised up by about 26% for 2015 after multinationals moved intellectual property and aircraft leasing assets to Ireland; employment and household incomes did not jump.

At market exchange rates US GDP is larger than China's, but the IMF estimates China's GDP at PPP has exceeded the USA's since about 2016.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that official GDP statistics significantly understate economic activity in developing countries.
items.answer: GDP is likely understated where informality is high, so comparisons over time are more reliable than comparisons of levels between countries.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large informal sectors are hard to record; subsistence agriculture and household production are unmeasured; out-of-date base years (e.g. Nigeria before 2014). Arguments against: statistical offices estimate informal output using surveys; some activity is also overstated (e.g. MNC transfer pricing); understatement also exists in high-income countries. Judgement: GDP is likely understated where informality is high, so comparisons over time are more reliable than comparisons of levels between countries. Reward explicit use of the extract. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Nominal GDP is $550 bn and the GDP deflator is 125. What is real GDP?
Priya writes: "If the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 110, real GDP must have fallen by 10%." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The deflator shows the price level; real GDP depends on nominal GDP as well. If nominal GDP rose by more than 10%, real GDP rose.
items.markingKey: The deflator shows the price level; real GDP depends on nominal GDP as well. If nominal GDP rose by more than 10%, real GDP rose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why economists use real rather than nominal GDP to measure economic growth.
items.answer: Nominal GDP can rise purely because prices rise; real GDP removes inflation so changes reflect changes in the volume of goods and services produced. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nominal GDP can rise purely because prices rise; real GDP removes inflation so changes reflect changes in the volume of goods and services produced. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In 2016, the value of all final output in Kalimar at current prices was $539 bn. The price index used to deflate GDP was 104 (base year = 100). Calculate real GDP.
items.markingKey: Real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 / deflator = 539 × 100 / 104 = 518.3. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for $518.3 bn. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: In Varnia, nominal GDP is $456 bn and real GDP (at base-year prices) is $365 bn. Calculate the GDP deflator and state what it shows about the price level since the base year.
items.answer: Deflator = 124.9; the average price level of domestic output is about 24.9% higher than in the base year.
items.markingKey: Deflator = nominal/real × 100 = 456/365 × 100 = 124.9. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 124.9. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [R1] interpretation relative to base year = 100.

items.stem: In 2022 nominal GDP was $600 bn with a deflator of 120; in 2023 nominal GDP was $660 bn with a deflator of 126. The population grew from 30 million to 30.6 million. Calculate the change in real GDP per capita and comment on the result.
items.answer: Real GDP 500 → 523.8 bn (+4.76%); per capita $16,667 → $17,118, a rise of about 2.7%. Nominal growth of 10% overstated the improvement; per capita real growth is more modest.
items.markingKey: Real GDP 500 → 523.8 bn (+4.76%); per capita $16,667 → $17,118, a rise of about 2.7%. Nominal growth of 10% overstated the improvement; per capita real growth is more modest.

items.stem: Which of the following is the formula for real GDP?
items.answer: Nominal GDP × 100 / price deflator
items.markingKey: D. Dividing by the deflator (÷100) removes the effect of price changes.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the GDP deflator and the consumer price index.
items.answer: The GDP deflator covers the prices of all domestically produced final output (including investment and government goods, excluding imports); the CPI covers a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical households, including imports.
items.markingKey: The GDP deflator covers the prices of all domestically produced final output (including investment and government goods, excluding imports); the CPI covers a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical households, including imports. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Zimbabwe in 2008 as an example, explain the importance of distinguishing real from nominal values.
items.answer: With annual inflation estimated in the hundreds of millions of per cent in 2008, nominal values became meaningless while real output collapsed. Nominal GDP soared while real GDP fell, so only deflated data showed the true fall in production
items.markingKey: Context (With annual inflation estimated in the hundreds of millions of per cent in 2008, nominal values became meaningless while real output collapsed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Nominal GDP soared while real GDP fell, so only deflated data showed the true fall in production – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of distinguishing real from nominal values.

items.stem: "If the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 110, real GDP must have fallen by 10%." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The deflator shows the price level; real GDP depends on nominal GDP as well. If nominal GDP rose by more than 10%, real GDP rose.
items.markingKey: The deflator shows the price level; real GDP depends on nominal GDP as well. If nominal GDP rose by more than 10%, real GDP rose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that real GDP per capita is an adequate measure of changes in a country's economic well-being over time.
items.answer: It is a necessary but not sufficient measure; changes in inequality, sustainability and non-income indicators must also be considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: removes inflation and population effects; data are widely available and comparable over time; strongly correlated with health and education outcomes. Arguments against: ignores distribution; ignores environmental degradation and resource depletion; excludes unpaid and informal work; ignores leisure and quality of goods. Supported judgement: It is a necessary but not sufficient measure; changes in inequality, sustainability and non-income indicators must also be considered. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "business cycle".
items.answer: The short-term fluctuations of real GDP around its long-term growth trend, consisting of expansion, peak, contraction and trough
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the short-term fluctuations of real GDP around its long-term growth trend, consisting of expansion, peak, contraction and trough. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why unemployment tends to rise during the contraction phase of the business cycle.
items.answer: Falling AD reduces firms' sales; as labour is a derived demand, firms cut output and jobs, so cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment rises.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Falling AD reduces firms' sales; as labour is a derived demand, firms cut output and jobs, so cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment rises. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A recession means that real GDP is negative." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A recession means that real GDP growth is negative (output falls) for two consecutive quarters; the level of GDP remains positive.
items.markingKey: A recession means that real GDP growth is negative (output falls) for two consecutive quarters; the level of GDP remains positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The OECD estimates that Tarsia's potential output is $434 bn, while actual real GDP is $447 bn. Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential output, and state what type of gap it is and one likely consequence.
items.answer: Output gap = (447 − 434)/434 × 100 = 3.0%: a positive (inflationary) output gap. Likely consequence: inflationary pressure as resources are over-used.
items.markingKey: (447 − 434)/434 × 100 = 3.0%. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 3.0%. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [A1] positive (inflationary) output gap; [R1] consequence.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the business cycle, showing the long-term growth trend and the phases of expansion, peak, contraction and trough, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Real GDP on the y-axis against time; fluctuating line around an upward-sloping trend line; label peak, contraction (recession), trough, expansion (recovery); explain that actual output deviates from potential output, creating positive and negative output gaps.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Real GDP on the y-axis against time; fluctuating line around an upward-sloping trend line; label peak, contraction (recession), trough, expansion (recovery); explain that actual output deviates from potential output, creating positive and negative output gaps. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that governments should aim to eliminate the business cycle.
items.answer: Governments should aim to smooth rather than eliminate the cycle, using automatic stabilisers and credible monetary policy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: recessions cause unemployment, lost output and hysteresis; booms cause inflation and asset bubbles; stable growth improves business confidence and investment. Arguments against: cycles are partly caused by supply shocks governments cannot control; policy has time lags and may destabilise; some fluctuation reallocates resources to more productive uses. Supported judgement: Governments should aim to smooth rather than eliminate the cycle, using automatic stabilisers and credible monetary policy.

items.stem: Which of the following would shift the long-term growth trend upwards?
options: A temporary rise in consumer confidence
An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
A fall in interest rates for one quarter
items.answer: An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
items.markingKey: C. The trend reflects growth in potential output (LRAS).

items.stem: Explain why the long-term growth trend can be shown on a PPC diagram as an outward shift.
items.answer: The trend reflects increases in productive capacity from more or better factors of production and technology, which shift the production possibilities curve outward (and LRAS to the right).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The trend reflects increases in productive capacity from more or better factors of production and technology, which shift the production possibilities curve outward (and LRAS to the right). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the 2008-2009 global financial crisis, explain how it illustrates the contraction phase of the business cycle.
items.answer: Real GDP in the USA fell for four consecutive quarters from mid-2008 and unemployment rose from under 5% to 10% by October 2009. The fall in household wealth and credit reduced C and I, AD fell, output fell below potential and cyclical unemployment rose
items.markingKey: Context (Real GDP in the USA fell for four consecutive quarters from mid-2008 and unemployment rose from under 5% to 10% by October 2009.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The fall in household wealth and credit reduced C and I, AD fell, output fell below potential and cyclical unemployment rose – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the contraction phase of the business cycle.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the business cycle, showing the long-term growth trend and the phases of expansion, peak, contraction and trough.
items.answer: Real GDP on the y-axis against time; fluctuating line around an upward-sloping trend line; label peak, contraction (recession), trough, expansion (recovery); explain that actual output deviates from potential output, creating positive and negative output gaps.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Real GDP on the y-axis against time; fluctuating line around an upward-sloping trend line; label peak, contraction (recession), trough, expansion (recovery); explain that actual output deviates from potential output, creating positive and negative output gaps. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Real GDP of an economy was $500 bn in 2020, $490 bn in 2021, $505 bn in 2022 and $530 bn in 2023, while potential output grew by 2% a year from $510 bn in 2020. Calculate the output gap in 2020 and 2023 and describe how the economy moved through the business cycle.
items.answer: 2020: (500 − 510)/510 = −2.0%; potential 2023 = 510 × 1.02³ ≈ 541.2, gap = (530 − 541.2)/541.2 ≈ −2.1%. Contraction in 2021 (−2%), trough 2021, then recovery/expansion in 2022-23, but output remains below potential (negative gap).
items.markingKey: 2020: (500 − 510)/510 = −2.0%; potential 2023 = 510 × 1.02³ ≈ 541.2, gap = (530 − 541.2)/541.2 ≈ −2.1%. Contraction in 2021 (−2%), trough 2021, then recovery/expansion in 2022-23, but output remains below potential (negative gap).

items.stem: Define the term "OECD Better Life Index".
items.answer: An interactive composite index that compares well-being across OECD countries using 11 dimensions such as housing, income, jobs, community, education, environment, health and life satisfaction
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an interactive composite index that compares well-being across OECD countries using 11 dimensions such as housing, income, jobs, community, education, environment, health and life satisfaction. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the OECD Better Life Index and GDP.
items.answer: GDP is a single monetary measure of market output; the Better Life Index is a multidimensional measure of well-being across 11 dimensions, which users can weight according to their own priorities.
items.markingKey: GDP is a single monetary measure of market output; the Better Life Index is a multidimensional measure of well-being across 11 dimensions, which users can weight according to their own priorities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that countries with the highest GDP per capita always have the happiest citizens. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Happiness rises with income but at a diminishing rate; social support, freedom, health and trust matter too, so the World Happiness Report ranking differs from the GDP ranking (e.g. Finland ranks first though not richest).
items.markingKey: Happiness rises with income but at a diminishing rate; social support, freedom, health and trust matter too, so the World Happiness Report ranking differs from the GDP ranking (e.g. Finland ranks first though not richest). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Countries with the highest GDP per capita always have the happiest citizens." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Happiness rises with income but at a diminishing rate; social support, freedom, health and trust matter too, so the World Happiness Report ranking differs from the GDP ranking (e.g. Finland ranks first though not richest).
items.markingKey: Happiness rises with income but at a diminishing rate; social support, freedom, health and trust matter too, so the World Happiness Report ranking differs from the GDP ranking (e.g. Finland ranks first though not richest). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that composite indicators such as the Happy Planet Index should replace GDP as the main measure of economic success.
items.answer: They should complement, not replace, GDP: a dashboard of indicators gives the fullest picture.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: capture well-being, health and sustainability; encourage sustainable policy; GDP counts harmful activity as positive. Arguments against: weighting of components is subjective; subjective well-being surveys are culturally biased; GDP is needed for macro policy, tax and debt analysis; composite measures are published infrequently. Supported judgement: They should complement, not replace, GDP: a dashboard of indicators gives the fullest picture.

items.stem: Briefly explain why GDP may be an inaccurate indicator of economic well-being.
items.answer: It excludes non-market output, the informal economy, leisure and the quality of goods; it ignores distribution and counts "defensive" spending (e.g. pollution clean-up) and environmental depletion as positive output.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It excludes non-market output, the informal economy, leisure and the quality of goods; it ignores distribution and counts "defensive" spending (e.g. pollution clean-up) and environmental depletion as positive output. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Because GDP ignores the environment, it should never be used." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: GDP remains useful for measuring output, cycles and tax capacity; the point is to supplement it with environmental and well-being indicators.
items.markingKey: GDP remains useful for measuring output, cycles and tax capacity; the point is to supplement it with environmental and well-being indicators. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Bhutan measures progress through a GNH index across nine domains, including psychological well-being, ecological diversity and good governance.

items.stem: An economy has C = 315, I = 116, G = 86, X = 180 and M = 148 ($ bn). What is GDP?
items.markingKey: C. GDP = C + I + G + X − M = 549.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Real GDP divided by the population; average inflation-adjusted output per person"?
items.answer: real GDP per capita
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of real GDP per capita.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "long-term growth trend".
items.answer: The average rate of growth of real GDP over a long period, reflecting the growth of potential output
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the average rate of growth of real GDP over a long period, reflecting the growth of potential output. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Because GDP ignores the environment, it should never be used." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: GDP remains useful for measuring output, cycles and tax capacity; the point is to supplement it with environmental and well-being indicators.
items.markingKey: GDP remains useful for measuring output, cycles and tax capacity; the point is to supplement it with environmental and well-being indicators. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between GNI and GDP.
items.answer: GDP measures output produced within the country's borders; GNI measures income earned by the country's residents, so it adds income received from abroad and subtracts income paid to non-residents.
items.markingKey: GDP measures output produced within the country's borders; GNI measures income earned by the country's residents, so it adds income received from abroad and subtracts income paid to non-residents. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the choice of base year can affect measured real GDP growth.
items.answer: Real GDP weights each good by base-year prices; goods whose relative prices have fallen sharply (e.g. electronics) get too much or too little weight if the base year is old, so statistical agencies rebase or use chain-linked indices.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Real GDP weights each good by base-year prices; goods whose relative prices have fallen sharply (e.g. electronics) get too much or too little weight if the base year is old, so statistical agencies rebase or use chain-linked indices. items.stem: Distinguish between actual growth and potential growth.
items.answer: Actual growth is the increase in real GDP produced; potential growth is the increase in the economy's capacity to produce, shown by an outward PPC shift or rightward LRAS shift.
items.markingKey: Actual growth is the increase in real GDP produced; potential growth is the increase in the economy's capacity to produce, shown by an outward PPC shift or rightward LRAS shift. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between GDP and the OECD Better Life Index.
items.answer: GDP is a single monetary measure of market output; the Better Life Index is a multidimensional measure of well-being across 11 dimensions, which users can weight according to their own priorities.
items.markingKey: GDP is a single monetary measure of market output; the Better Life Index is a multidimensional measure of well-being across 11 dimensions, which users can weight according to their own priorities. items.stem: Hana writes: "Nominal GDP rose by 8% so the economy produced 8% more goods and services." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Nominal GDP includes price changes; if inflation was, say, 6%, real output rose only by about 2%.
items.markingKey: Nominal GDP includes price changes; if inflation was, say, 6%, real output rose only by about 2%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Zimbabwe in 2008 and explain what it reveals about the importance of distinguishing real from nominal values.
items.answer: With annual inflation estimated in the hundreds of millions of per cent in 2008, nominal values became meaningless while real output collapsed. Nominal GDP soared while real GDP fell, so only deflated data showed the true fall in production
items.markingKey: Context (With annual inflation estimated in the hundreds of millions of per cent in 2008, nominal values became meaningless while real output collapsed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Nominal GDP soared while real GDP fell, so only deflated data showed the true fall in production – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of distinguishing real from nominal values.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the 2008-2009 global financial crisis shows the contraction phase of the business cycle.
items.answer: Real GDP in the USA fell for four consecutive quarters from mid-2008 and unemployment rose from under 5% to 10% by October 2009. The fall in household wealth and credit reduced C and I, AD fell, output fell below potential and cyclical unemployment rose
items.markingKey: Context (Real GDP in the USA fell for four consecutive quarters from mid-2008 and unemployment rose from under 5% to 10% by October 2009.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The fall in household wealth and credit reduced C and I, AD fell, output fell below potential and cyclical unemployment rose – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the contraction phase of the business cycle.

items.stem: Using China's attempt to publish a green GDP in 2006 as an example, explain alternative measures that account for the environment.
items.answer: China's first green GDP report estimated environmental costs at about 3% of GDP in 2004, but the project was shelved after provincial officials objected. Subtracting pollution costs lowers measured growth, revealing the trade-off between rapid growth and environmental quality
items.markingKey: Context (China's first green GDP report estimated environmental costs at about 3% of GDP in 2004, but the project was shelved after provincial officials objected.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A student claims that real GDP is always smaller than nominal GDP. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only after the base year when prices have risen; before the base year, or if prices fall (deflation), real GDP can exceed nominal GDP.
items.markingKey: Only after the base year when prices have risen; before the base year, or if prices fall (deflation), real GDP can exceed nominal GDP. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using China's growth since 1980 as an example, explain the long-term growth trend.
items.answer: China averaged close to 10% annual real GDP growth from 1980 to 2010, slowing to around 5% in the 2020s. Rapid accumulation of capital, rural-urban migration and technology transfer raised potential output, but the trend rate slows as catch-up opportunities shrink
items.markingKey: Context (China averaged close to 10% annual real GDP growth from 1980 to 2010, slowing to around 5% in the 2020s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rapid accumulation of capital, rural-urban migration and technology transfer raised potential output, but the trend rate slows as catch-up opportunities shrink – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the long-term growth trend.

items.stem: With reference to Finland's top ranking in the World Happiness Report, explain how it illustrates the limitations of GDP as a measure of well-being.
items.answer: Finland has ranked first in the World Happiness Report every year from 2018 to 2025, despite a GDP per capita lower than those of Norway, Switzerland or the USA. High social trust, social support, low corruption and strong public services raise life evaluations beyond what income alone predicts
items.markingKey: Context (Finland has ranked first in the World Happiness Report every year from 2018 to 2025, despite a GDP per capita lower than those of Norway, Switzerland or the USA.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High social trust, social support, low corruption and strong public services raise life evaluations beyond what income alone predicts – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limitations of GDP as a measure of well-being.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that gNI per capita at PPP is the most useful single measure for comparing living standards between countries.
items.answer: It is the best single monetary measure, but comparisons should be supplemented by composite indicators such as the HDI and by inequality data.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: adjusts for population size; adjusts for price-level differences; includes net income from abroad, reflecting residents' incomes. Arguments against: ignores distribution of income; excludes non-market and informal output; ignores environmental costs, leisure and quality of life; PPP estimates rely on price surveys that may be inaccurate. Supported judgement: It is the best single monetary measure, but comparisons should be supplemented by composite indicators such as the HDI and by inequality data.

items.stem: You are an economist at the trade ministry. A minister argues that governments should aim to eliminate the business cycle. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Governments should aim to smooth rather than eliminate the cycle, using automatic stabilisers and credible monetary policy.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: recessions cause unemployment, lost output and hysteresis; booms cause inflation and asset bubbles; stable growth improves business confidence and investment. Counter-points: cycles are partly caused by supply shocks governments cannot control; policy has time lags and may destabilise; some fluctuation reallocates resources to more productive uses. Recommendation: Governments should aim to smooth rather than eliminate the cycle, using automatic stabilisers and credible monetary policy. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "GDP divided by the population, giving average output (income) per person"?
items.answer: GDP per capita
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of GDP per capita.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Prices of a fixed base year used to value output so that only changes in quantity are measured"?
items.answer: constant prices
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of constant prices.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The real GDP an economy could produce when all its resources are fully employed at the natural rate of unemployment"?
items.answer: potential output

items.stem: Explain the difference between total GDP and GDP per capita.
items.answer: Total GDP is the size of the whole economy; GDP per capita divides by population, so it shows average output per person and allows living-standard comparisons.
items.markingKey: Total GDP is the size of the whole economy; GDP per capita divides by population, so it shows average output per person and allows living-standard comparisons. items.stem: Distinguish between the consumer price index and the GDP deflator.
items.answer: The GDP deflator covers the prices of all domestically produced final output (including investment and government goods, excluding imports); the CPI covers a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical households, including imports.
items.markingKey: The GDP deflator covers the prices of all domestically produced final output (including investment and government goods, excluding imports); the CPI covers a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical households, including imports. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "During an expansion the economy is always above its long-term trend." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: An expansion begins at a trough below trend; output may still be below potential (negative output gap) for much of the recovery.
items.markingKey: An expansion begins at a trough below trend; output may still be below potential (negative output gap) for much of the recovery. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Happy Planet Index can rank a middle-income country such as Costa Rica above high-income countries.
items.answer: HPI rewards high well-being and life expectancy achieved with a small ecological footprint; Costa Rica achieves high life satisfaction and long lives with low resource use, while many rich countries have very large footprints.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: HPI rewards high well-being and life expectancy achieved with a small ecological footprint; Costa Rica achieves high life satisfaction and long lives with low resource use, while many rich countries have very large footprints. items.stem: Briefly describe the comparison of China and the USA using PPP and explain what it reveals about purchasing power parity.
items.answer: At market exchange rates US GDP is larger than China's, but the IMF estimates China's GDP at PPP has exceeded the USA's since about 2016. Lower prices of non-traded goods in China mean each yuan buys more, so PPP raises China's measured output relative to market-rate figures

Using the common definition, identify when the economy entered recession, and explain which phase of the business cycle the economy was in at the end of the period.
items.answer: A recession (two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth) began in Q2 2022 and lasted to Q3 2022. At the end (Q4 2023, growth +1.1%) the economy was in an expansion/recovery phase.
